source.title: Holistic Scaling Laws for Optimal Mixture-of-Experts Architecture Optimization
source.authors: Weilin Wan; Jin Han; Wei-Zhong Zhang; Cheng Jin

record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling-law measurements to MoE language models, sweeping compute and architectural configurations and reporting pretraining-loss results.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling fits and loss comparisons. It also reports a median-d proxy correlation as a validation of its search method; that is recorded under fits_no_version because correlation with the true minimum loss is not itself one of the listed claim versions. Results cited from other papers are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own ~670 MoE language models from 10^18 to 3×10^20 FLOPs. It reports loss-versus-compute power-law fits (V1), a refit of compute-optimal FLOPs-per-token and token allocation (V3), and loss sensitivity to shape at fixed (M, Na, N) (V4). It also compares two fit forms whose extrapolations diverge (V7). This is a new setting (fine-grained MoE, 288 experts, top-8) with results on the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that their decomposition yields compute-conditioned scaling laws mapping any budget to a full optimal MoE architecture (M, D, Na, N, d), and that the near-optimal band widens with scale. They acknowledge six scales, a fixed Ne/K, (C, M, D) laws fit with heuristic architectures, and loss-only evaluation.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains MoE models and jointly searches architecture variables, using its own data and infrastructure. It applies a compute-scaling setup informed by prior work but does not reproduce the original dense-model experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The loss-versus-compute extrapolation depends on whether a loss floor is included; the paper reports little fit difference within the tested range but divergence beyond it. Results are also conditional on the tested MoE width ratio, fixed Ne=288 and K=8, and six compute scales.

fits_no_version.finding: The median-feasible-d proxy loss tracks the minimum loss over d. Pearson r=0.98 at 1e18, and 0.95–0.99 across scales (Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed (M, Na, N), hidden dimension changes loss far less than macroscopic allocation does, preserving configuration rankings.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimal hidden dimension grows with compute as d = 1262.8 + 41.1·C^0.092.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal MoE shape parameters follow offset power laws in compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimal total/active ratio N/Na rises slowly (19.2 to 22.1), with loss within 1% over N/Na 18–25.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE expansion ratio has a flat, slowly drifting optimum across compute.

record.problems: Only six compute scales are tested, limiting confidence in extrapolation. The fitted (C,M,D) laws use heuristic architectures and are not refitted after architecture optimization. All experiments fix Ne=288 and K=8. Evaluation is limited to pretraining cross-entropy; downstream transfer is unresolved. The paper notes early reruns of identical configurations had absolute loss fluctuation of approximately 0.005, but does not report per-configuration multi-seed uncertainty.

untested.parts: Loss is fit against compute only, along compute-optimal points, over about 2.5 orders of magnitude. There are no separate laws in parameters or tokens. Held-out status is not stated.
Fits are extrapolated to 10^22–10^23 FLOPs but never checked against larger runs.
Allocation is expressed via FLOPs per token (M), not parameter count. No uncertainty or underlying data is shown for Eq. (2). Only one sparsity setting is used (Ne=288, K=8).
Only d and the MoE FFN width ratio are varied, in one MoE family. There is no broad depth/width sweep and no comparison across architecture families.
Not tested: only text pretraining is studied.
Parameter-counting rules, data, and schedules are not varied. Only the fit form is compared.

missing.what: Per-scale width-ratio loss spreads from the Fig. 10 labels, which exceed the text's '<0.5%' at small scales (E=0: 1.096%, 0.904%, 0.694%, 0.503%, 0.366%, 0.367%)
The extrapolated optimal width ratio differs between the E=0 and E≠0 fits at 10^21–10^23 FLOPs
Loss versus d quadratic fits per scale, plus the band endpoints dl and dr, which the paper says follow power laws in C
Cross-scale proxy validation correlations (Pearson 0.95–0.99 at six scales)

record.verdict_notes: r7–r16 compute exponents are on log L versus log C; the fits are presumably base-10, but no base is stated. Eq. (2) is presented as a refit 'following Hoffmann' with no data points or uncertainty shown. Reruns of identical configs fluctuate by about 0.005 in loss, which is comparable to the 0.1% bands (about 0.002 at L≈2.0). That makes the band widths and width-ratio differences near noise. The 8% shape variance in Kaplan et al. is cited, not measured here.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits pretraining cross-entropy against compute for MoE width-ratio groups. Whether the reported loss is held-out is not stated; it does not separately establish loss scaling in parameters or tokens with the other quantities non-bottlenecked.
The paper plots extrapolations beyond the trained compute range, but does not validate small-run predictions against larger runs held out from fitting.

It reports compute-optimal token and FLOPs-per-token fits and parameter-count outputs for six scales, but does not report a fitted power-law exponent for active or total parameter count itself. The experiment uses one fixed MoE sparsity setting.
The study varies hidden dimension and MoE FFN width ratio in its tested MoE setup. It does not test a broad range of depth, width, or architecture families.
Only text pretraining is studied; other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
Downstream performance is not evaluated; the paper says its relationship to the architecture-space loss landscape remains unresolved.

The paper compares two loss-versus-compute fit forms for MoE width-ratio groups and reports that their extrapolations diverge. It does not systematically vary parameter-counting rules, datasets, or training schedules to compare fitted laws.
